claim: Approximately 60% of melanoma tumors harbor a BRAF mutation, most often BRAFV600E.
source: Approximately, 60% of melanoma tumors harbor a BRAF mutation, most often BRAFV600E, which leads to hyperactivation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Davies et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davies et al., 2002

claim: BRAFV600E mutation leads to hyperactivation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
source: Approximately, 60% of melanoma tumors harbor a BRAF mutation, most often BRAFV600E, which leads to hyperactivation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway (Davies et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davies et al., 2002

claim: Drugs targeting the BRAF and MAPK pathways are clinically important, but almost invariably, resistance arises within a short time period.
source: Drugs targeting the BRAF and MAPK pathways are clinically important, but almost invariably, resistance arises within a short time period (Kugel and Aplin, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kugel and Aplin, 2014

claim: Melanoma inherits its aggressive nature from its multipotent neural crest precursors.
source: Melanoma inherits its aggressive nature from its multipotent neural crest precursors that gives rise to various cells including melanocytes, glia, and adrenal cells (Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999; Le Douarin and Dupin, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999; Le Douarin and Dupin, 2018

claim: Neural crest precursors give rise to various cells including melanocytes, glia, and adrenal cells.
source: Melanoma inherits its aggressive nature from its multipotent neural crest precursors that gives rise to various cells including melanocytes, glia, and adrenal cells (Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999; Le Douarin and Dupin, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999; Le Douarin and Dupin, 2018

claim: Dysregulation of neural crest genes is predictive of metastatic potential and negative prognosis in melanoma.
source: The developmental programme of neural crest cells is believed to be reinitiated during melanoma progression and dysregulation of neural crest genes is predictive of metastatic potential and negative prognosis in melanoma (Mascarenhas et al., 2010; Bailey et al., 2012; Kulesa et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mascarenhas et al., 2010; Bailey et al., 2012; Kulesa et al., 2006

claim: The rare germline mutation E318K of MITF increases the susceptibility to melanoma.
source: This is best evidenced by the observations that the rare germline mutation E318K of MITF increases the susceptibility to melanoma and MITF has been shown to be amplified in 15% of melanoma tumors (Bertolotto et al., 2011; Garraway et al., 2005; Yokoyama et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertolotto et al., 2011; Garraway et al., 2005; Yokoyama et al., 2011

claim: MITF has been shown to be amplified in 15% of melanoma tumors.
source: This is best evidenced by the observations that the rare germline mutation E318K of MITF increases the susceptibility to melanoma and MITF has been shown to be amplified in 15% of melanoma tumors (Bertolotto et al., 2011; Garraway et al., 2005; Yokoyama et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bertolotto et al., 2011; Garraway et al., 2005; Yokoyama et al., 2011

claim: MITFhigh cells are characterized as proliferative.
source: Importantly, MITF activity has been used as a proxy for the phenotype switching model with MITFhigh cells characterized as proliferative, whereas MITFlow cells have been assigned a quiescent invasive phenotype (Carreira et al., 2006; Hoek et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carreira et al., 2006; Hoek et al., 2006

claim: MITFlow cells have been assigned a quiescent invasive phenotype.
source: Importantly, MITF activity has been used as a proxy for the phenotype switching model with MITFhigh cells characterized as proliferative, whereas MITFlow cells have been assigned a quiescent invasive phenotype (Carreira et al., 2006; Hoek et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carreira et al., 2006; Hoek et al., 2006

claim: Cells lacking MITF are abundant in melanomas.
source: However, antibody staining suggests that cells lacking MITF are abundant in melanomas (Goodall et al., 2008) and single-cell sequencing of human xenotransplants and of zebrafish melanoma models suggest the existence of cells with very low MITF expression (Rambow et al., 2018; Travnickova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodall et al., 2008; Rambow et al., 2018; Travnickova et al., 2019

claim: Single-cell sequencing of human xenotransplants and of zebrafish melanoma models suggest the existence of cells with very low MITF expression.
source: However, antibody staining suggests that cells lacking MITF are abundant in melanomas (Goodall et al., 2008) and single-cell sequencing of human xenotransplants and of zebrafish melanoma models suggest the existence of cells with very low MITF expression (Rambow et al., 2018; Travnickova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rambow et al., 2018; Travnickova et al., 2019

claim: Expression of ECM proteins such as tenascin and fibronectin increases during melanoma disease progression.
source: In melanoma, expression of ECM proteins such as tenascin and fibronectin increases during disease progression (Frey et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frey et al., 2011

claim: Focal adhesions offer physical attachment of cells to the ECM through the integrin receptor.
source: Focal adhesions not only offer physical attachment of cells to the ECM through the integrin receptor, but also initiate signaling cascades that regulate cell proliferation, migration, and survival (Mitra et al., 2005; Geiger et al., 2001; Playford and Schaller, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitra et al., 2005; Geiger et al., 2001; Playford and Schaller, 2004

claim: Focal adhesions initiate signaling cascades that regulate cell proliferation, migration, and survival.
source: Focal adhesions not only offer physical attachment of cells to the ECM through the integrin receptor, but also initiate signaling cascades that regulate cell proliferation, migration, and survival (Mitra et al., 2005; Geiger et al., 2001; Playford and Schaller, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitra et al., 2005; Geiger et al., 2001; Playford and Schaller, 2004

claim: Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) activates the ERK pathway via Grb-FAK interactions.
source: A key focal adhesion signaling protein is Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK), which activates the ERK pathway via Grb-FAK interactions (Schlaepfer et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schlaepfer et al., 1999

claim: Paxillin (PXN) recruits other proteins to the focal adhesion sites when phosphorylated by FAK and SRC.
source: An important scaffolding protein at the focal adhesion complex is Paxillin (PXN) which recruits other proteins to the focal adhesion sites when phosphorylated by FAK and SRC (Deakin and Turner, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deakin and Turner, 2008

claim: Phosphorylation of PXN is critical for activation of RAF, MEK, and ERK.
source: Importantly, phosphorylation of PXN is critical for activation of RAF, MEK, and ERK and has been shown to confer drug resistance by activating Bcl-2 through ERK signaling (Wu et al., 2016; Sen et al., 2010; Ishibe et al., 2003; Sen et al., 2012; Hirata et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2016; Sen et al., 2010; Ishibe et al., 2003; Sen et al., 2012; Hirata et al., 2015

claim: Phosphorylation of PXN has been shown to confer drug resistance by activating Bcl-2 through ERK signaling.
source: Importantly, phosphorylation of PXN is critical for activation of RAF, MEK, and ERK and has been shown to confer drug resistance by activating Bcl-2 through ERK signaling (Wu et al., 2016; Sen et al., 2010; Ishibe et al., 2003; Sen et al., 2012; Hirata et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2016; Sen et al., 2010; Ishibe et al., 2003; Sen et al., 2012; Hirata et al., 2015

claim: MITF directly represses the expression of genes associated with the extracellular matrix (ECM) and focal adhesion pathways in human melanoma cells.
source: Here, we show that MITF directly represses the expression of genes associated with the extracellular matrix (ECM) and focal adhesion pathways in human melanoma cells as well as of regulators of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) such as CDH2, thus affecting cell morphology and cell-matrix interactions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from MITF knockout, knockdown, and overexpression studies, as well as CUT-and-RUN and ChIP-seq data showing direct MITF binding

claim: MITF directly represses the expression of regulators of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) such as CDH2.
source: Here, we show that MITF directly represses the expression of genes associated with the extracellular matrix (ECM) and focal adhesion pathways in human melanoma cells as well as of regulators of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) such as CDH2, thus affecting cell morphology and cell-matrix interactions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased CDH2 expression upon MITF loss and MITF binding to CDH2 regulatory regions

claim: MITF affects cell morphology and cell-matrix interactions.
source: Here, we show that MITF directly represses the expression of genes associated with the extracellular matrix (ECM) and focal adhesion pathways in human melanoma cells as well as of regulators of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) such as CDH2, thus affecting cell morphology and cell-matrix interactions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing morphological changes and altered matrigel interactions in MITF-KO cells

claim: The effects of MITF on ECM and focal adhesion genes are reversible.
source: Importantly, we show that these effects of MITF are reversible, as expected from the rheostat model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from rescue experiments and doxycycline-inducible MITF knockdown/restoration studies

claim: The number of focal adhesion points increased upon MITF knockdown.
source: The number of focal adhesion points increased upon MITF knockdown, a feature observed in drug-resistant melanomas.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing increased paxillin-positive focal points in MITF-KO and MITF-KD cells

claim: Increased focal adhesion points is a feature observed in drug-resistant melanomas.
source: The number of focal adhesion points increased upon MITF knockdown, a feature observed in drug-resistant melanomas.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on drug resistance and focal adhesions

claim: Cells lacking MITF are similar to the cells of minimal residual disease observed in both human and zebrafish melanomas.
source: Cells lacking MITF are similar to the cells of minimal residual disease observed in both human and zebrafish melanomas.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis showing enrichment of MRD gene signatures in MITF-KO cells

claim: MITF plays a critical role as a repressor of gene expression in melanoma cells.
source: Our results suggest that MITF plays a critical role as a repressor of gene expression and is actively involved in shaping the microenvironment of melanoma cells in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN and ChIP-seq data showing direct MITF binding to repressed genes, and transcriptomic data showing gene expression changes

claim: MITF is actively involved in shaping the microenvironment of melanoma cells in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Our results suggest that MITF plays a critical role as a repressor of gene expression and is actively involved in shaping the microenvironment of melanoma cells in a cell-autonomous manner.
evidence: Supported by data showing MITF regulates ECM gene expression in isolated melanoma cells

claim: The ΔMITF-X2 line had two different but independent insertion mutations in the same codon (insertion of A and T in the codon for Y22) and a 5 bp deletion (encoding Y22 and H23) that are present in 64%, 19%, and 17% of sequenced DNA fragments in this region, respectively.
source: The ΔMITF-X2 line had two different but independent insertion mutations in the same codon (insertion of A and T in the codon for Y22) and a 5 bp deletion (encoding Y22 and H23) that are present in 64%, 19%, and 17% of sequenced DNA fragments in this region, respectively.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing and Sanger sequencing data

claim: All mutations in the ΔMITF-X2 line introduced frameshifts and premature stop codons in exon 2 of MITF.
source: All these mutations introduced frameshifts and premature stop codons in exon 2 of MITF (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data and shown in Figure 1b

claim: The mutations present in the ΔMITF-X6 line are: 52% of the sequenced fragments contained a deletion of 1 bp (encoding residue A198), 33% contained a 6 bp in-frame deletion in the basic domain of the protein (encoding residues R197-R198), and 15% of the sequenced fragments contained a 17 bp deletion (encoding residues 198–203).
source: The mutations present in the ΔMITF-X6 line are the following: 52% of the sequenced fragments contained a deletion of 1 bp (encoding residue A198), 33% contained a 6 bp in-frame deletion in the basic domain of the protein (encoding residues R197-R198), and 15% of the sequenced fragments contained a 17 bp deletion (encoding residues 198–203).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data

claim: Both the 1- and 17 bp deletions in ΔMITF-X6 introduced frameshifts and downstream stop codons.
source: Both the 1- and 17 bp deletions introduced frameshifts and downstream stop codons (Figure 1c), whereas the in-frame 6 bp deletion removed two amino acids at the beginning of the alpha-helix encoding the basic domain and is therefore not expected to be able to bind DNA.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data and shown in Figure 1c

claim: The in-frame 6 bp deletion in ΔMITF-X6 removed two amino acids at the beginning of the alpha-helix encoding the basic domain and is therefore not expected to be able to bind DNA.
source: Both the 1- and 17 bp deletions introduced frameshifts and downstream stop codons (Figure 1c), whereas the in-frame 6 bp deletion removed two amino acids at the beginning of the alpha-helix encoding the basic domain and is therefore not expected to be able to bind DNA.
evidence: Based on inference from the location of the deletion in the DNA-binding domain

claim: No wild-type MITF gene was detected in either ΔMITF-X2 or ΔMITF-X6 cell line.
source: No wild-type MITF gene was detected in either cell line.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data

claim: Western blotting revealed that the ΔMITF-X6 cells express very little, if any, MITF protein.
source: Western blotting revealed that the ΔMITF-X6 cells express very little, if any, MITF protein.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1d

claim: The ΔMITF-X2 cells did not express the full-length ~55 kDa MITF protein, but truncated forms of MITF were detected at ~40 and 47 kDa.
source: Although the ΔMITF-X2 cells did not express the full-length ~55 kDa MITF protein, truncated forms of MITF were detected at ~40 and 47 kDa (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1d

claim: Truncated MITF forms at ~40 and 47 kDa were also present in wild-type cells, albeit at lower levels.
source: These truncated forms were also present in wild-type cells, albeit at lower levels, suggesting that these are alternative isoforms of the MITF protein (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1d

claim: The truncated MITF proteins in ΔMITF-X2 cells are most likely products of alternative translation start sites.
source: Similarly, neither the WGS nor RT-PCR studies showed evidence for transcripts lacking exon2 from the ∆MITF-X2 cDNA indicating that the truncated MITF proteins are most likely products of alternative translation start sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Based on inference from WGS and RT-PCR data showing no alternative splicing

claim: Both MITF-KO cell lines exhibited enlarged cytoplasm as compared to controls.
source: Morphological analysis revealed that both MITF-KO cell lines exhibited enlarged cytoplasm as compared to controls (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1e-g

claim: The average size of the ΔMITF-X2 and ΔMITF-X6 cells was 1.7-fold larger than the EV-SkMel28 cells.
source: Quantification of phase-contrast microscopy images revealed that the average size of the ΔMITF-X2 and ΔMITF-X6 cells was 1.7-fold larger than the EV-SkMel28 cells (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by quantification of microscopy images shown in Figure 1g

claim: Both MITF-KO cell lines formed aggregates when seeded on top of matrigel-coated slides, whereas the control EV-SkMel28 cells displayed a flat sheet-like morphology.
source: Both MITF-KO cell lines formed aggregates, whereas the control EV-SkMel28 cells displayed a flat sheet-like morphology (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1h

claim: 2136 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified between ΔMITF-X6 and EV-SkMel28 cells with the cut off qval <0.05.
source: We identified 2136 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between ΔMITF-X6 and EV-SkMel28 cells with the cut off qval <0.05 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Of the 2136 DEGs, 1516 genes showed twofold change in expression.
source: Of these, 1516 genes showed twofold change in expression (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2a

claim: Genes reduced in expression upon MITF depletion were verified MITF-target genes involved in pigmentation and pigment cell differentiation such as DCT, MLANA, OCA2, and IRF4 in addition to MITF itself.
source: Gene ontology and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the genes reduced in expression upon MITF depletion were verified MITF-target genes involved in pigmentation and pigment cell differentiation such as DCT, MLANA, OCA2, and IRF4 in addition to MITF itself (Figure 2a,b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and GO/KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: Genes whose expression was increased upon loss of MITF were enriched in processes involved in glycosaminoglycan metabolism, ECM organization and extracellular structure organization, and included genes such as SERPINA3, ITGA2, PXDN, and TGFβ1.
source: Genes whose expression was increased upon loss of MITF were enriched in processes involved in glycosaminoglycan metabolism, ECM organization and extracellular structure organization, and included genes such as SERPINA3, ITGA2, PXDN, and TGFβ1 (Figure 2a,b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and GO/KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 2a,b

claim: 37,643 MITF CUT-and-RUN peaks were identified located 10 kb +/- from the TSS, 3'UTR or intronic regions of 8288 genes.
source: We identified 37,643 peaks located 10 kb +/- from the TSS, 3'UTR or intronic regions of 8288 genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN sequencing data

claim: 695 of the 1284 induced genes associated with MITF peaks (p<7.3e-09 hypergeometric test).
source: We found that 695 of the 1284 induced genes (p<7.3e-09 hypergeometric test) and 535 of the 852 repressed genes (p<6.6e-23, hypergeometric test) associated with MITF peaks (Figure 2e; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by integration of RNA-seq and CUT-and-RUN data with statistical analysis

claim: 535 of the 852 repressed genes associated with MITF peaks (p<6.6e-23, hypergeometric test).
source: We found that 695 of the 1284 induced genes (p<7.3e-09 hypergeometric test) and 535 of the 852 repressed genes (p<6.6e-23, hypergeometric test) associated with MITF peaks (Figure 2e; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by integration of RNA-seq and CUT-and-RUN data with statistical analysis

claim: Of the 183 ECM and focal adhesion genes whose expression was increased upon MITF knockout, 101 were associated with MITF peaks and induced in expression upon loss of MITF.
source: Of the 183 ECM and focal adhesion genes whose expression was increased upon MITF knockout, 101 were associated with MITF peaks and induced in expression upon loss of MITF (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by integration of RNA-seq and CUT-and-RUN data

claim: 42 ECM genes were consistently bound by MITF in all three studies (SkMel28 CUT-and-RUN, COLO829 ChIP-seq, and 501Mel HA-MITF ChIP-seq).
source: We compared our MITF CUT and RUN peaks with the published MITF ChIP-seq data from COLO829 (generated using the same antibody as used here) (Supplementary file 3) and HA-MITF ChIP-seq 501Mel cells (Supplementary file 4) and found 42 ECM genes consistently bound by MITF in all three studies (Figure 2f,g; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by comparison of CUT-and-RUN and ChIP-seq datasets

claim: MITF peaks associated with induced genes (777) were primarily enriched for the 5'-CA[T/C]GTGAC-3' motif.
source: We found that MITF peaks associated with induced genes (777) were primarily enriched for the 5'-CA[T/C]GTGAC-3' motif, whereas those near reduced genes (535) were enriched for the 5'-CACATG-3' motif (Figure 2h).
evidence: Supported by de novo motif analysis using MEMEChIP shown in Figure 2h

claim: MITF peaks near reduced genes (535) were enriched for the 5'-CACATG-3' motif.
source: We found that MITF peaks associated with induced genes (777) were primarily enriched for the 5'-CA[T/C]GTGAC-3' motif, whereas those near reduced genes (535) were enriched for the 5'-CACATG-3' motif (Figure 2h).
evidence: Supported by de novo motif analysis using MEMEChIP shown in Figure 2h

claim: 1040 DEGs (q-val <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 567 induced, 473 reduced) were identified upon siRNA-mediated MITF depletion in SkMel28 cells compared to siCTRL.
source: We identified 1040 DEGs (q-val <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 567 induced, 473 reduced) upon siRNA-mediated MITF depletion in SkMel28 cells compared to siCTRL and 1114 DEGs in 501Mel cells (q-val <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 624 induced, 490 reduced) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from siRNA knockdown experiments

claim: 1114 DEGs were identified in 501Mel cells upon siRNA-mediated MITF depletion (q-val <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 624 induced, 490 reduced).
source: We identified 1040 DEGs (q-val <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 567 induced, 473 reduced) upon siRNA-mediated MITF depletion in SkMel28 cells compared to siCTRL and 1114 DEGs in 501Mel cells (q-val <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 624 induced, 490 reduced) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from siRNA knockdown experiments

claim: A significant correlation was observed between the DEGs of ΔMITF-X6 vs. EV-Skmel28 cells and DEGs of siMITF vs. siCTRL in SkMel28 (Pearson correlation = 0.66, p<2.2e-16).
source: A significant correlation was observed between the DEGs of ΔMITF-X6 vs. EV-Skmel28 cells and DEGs of siMITF vs. siCTRL in SkMel28 (Pearson correlation = 0.66, p<2.2e-16) and 501Mel cells (Pearson correlation = 0.57, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3a,b

claim: A significant correlation was observed between the DEGs of ΔMITF-X6 vs. EV-Skmel28 cells and DEGs of siMITF vs. siCTRL in 501Mel cells (Pearson correlation = 0.57, p<2.2e-16).
source: A significant correlation was observed between the DEGs of ΔMITF-X6 vs. EV-Skmel28 cells and DEGs of siMITF vs. siCTRL in SkMel28 (Pearson correlation = 0.66, p<2.2e-16) and 501Mel cells (Pearson correlation = 0.57, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3a,b

claim: 2655 DEGs (FDR < 0.01, log2FC≥|1|, 1835 induced and 820 reduced) were identified between MITFlow and MITFhigh tumors in TCGA.
source: By performing differential gene expression analysis between the two groups, we identified 2655 DEGs (FDR < 0.01, log2FC≥|1|, 1835 induced and 820 reduced) between MITFlow and MITFhigh tumors (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA melanoma tumor data

claim: The DEGs observed when comparing the ΔMITF-X6 cells to the EV-SkMel28 cells and the DEGs observed upon comparing the MITFlow and MITFhigh tumors were significantly correlated (R = 0.76, p<2.2e-16).
source: Interestingly, the DEGs observed when comparing the ΔMITF-X6 cells to the EV-SkMel28 cells and the DEGs observed upon comparing the MITFlow and MITFhigh tumors were significantly correlated (R = 0.76, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 3c

claim: MITFlow tumors cluster near the ΔMITF-X6 cells in principal component analysis.
source: Additionally, principal component analysis using the top 200 most statistically significant genes in each case revealed that MITFlow tumors cluster near the ΔMITF-X6 cells, whereas MITFhigh tumors cluster with EV-SkMEL28 cells, indicating that ΔMITF-X6 cells portray the transcriptional state of MITFlow tumors (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3e

claim: MITFhigh tumors cluster with EV-SkMEL28 cells in principal component analysis.
source: Additionally, principal component analysis using the top 200 most statistically significant genes in each case revealed that MITFlow tumors cluster near the ΔMITF-X6 cells, whereas MITFhigh tumors cluster with EV-SkMEL28 cells, indicating that ΔMITF-X6 cells portray the transcriptional state of MITFlow tumors (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3e

claim: 8110 DEGs (qval <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 4863 induced, 3247 reduced) were identified between pB-MITF-FLAG and pB-FLAG in A375P cells.
source: We identified 8110 DEGs (qval <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 4863 induced, 3247 reduced) between pB-MITF-FLAG and pB-FLAG in A375P cells and among genes that are decreased in expression are ECM-related genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from MITF overexpression experiments

claim: Among genes that are decreased in expression upon MITF overexpression in A375P cells are ECM-related genes.
source: We identified 8110 DEGs (qval <0.05, log2FC≥|1|, 4863 induced, 3247 reduced) between pB-MITF-FLAG and pB-FLAG in A375P cells and among genes that are decreased in expression are ECM-related genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from MITF overexpression experiments

claim: The DEGs observed upon MITF overexpression in A375P cells showed anti-correlation with the DEGs observed when comparing ΔMITF-X6 to EV-SkMel28 cells (Pearson correlation = −0.46, p<2.2e-16).
source: As expected, the DEGs observed upon MITF overexpression in A375P cells showed anti-correlation with the DEGs observed when comparing ΔMITF-X6 to EV-SkMel28 cells (Pearson correlation = −0.46, p<2.2e-16) (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 3d

claim: Overexpressing MITF in the A375P cell line led to a reduction in expression of ECM genes and induction of pigmentation and autophagy genes.
source: Conversely, overexpressing MITF in the A375P cell line led to a reduction in expression of ECM genes and induction of pigmentation and autophagy genes, again showing that MITF negatively regulates the expression of ECM genes (Figure 3f).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3f

claim: Overexpression of MITF led to the repression of 213 ECM genes, 82 of which were direct MITF targets.
source: In contrast, overexpression of MITF led to the repression of 213 ECM genes, 82 of which were direct MITF targets, indicating a major repressive influence of MITF on ECM gene expression (Figure 3g; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by integration of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3g

claim: Overexpression of MITF in dox-inducible A375P cells showed a significant reduction in the expression of LOXL2, MMP15, MMP2, and COL1A2 when compared to control pB-FLAG cells.
source: We confirmed the repressive effects of MITF by RT-qPCR in dox-inducible A375P cells overexpressing pB-MITF-FLAG, which showed a significant reduction in the expression of LOXL2, MMP15, MMP2, and COL1A2 when compared to control pB-FLAG cells (Figure 3h).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3h

claim: ECM genes are strongly enriched in MITFlow tumors in TCGA.
source: Interestingly, using GSEA analysis, we observed increased enrichment of ECM genes in the MITFlow tumors (Figure 3i).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 3i

claim: Expression of genes encoding ECM proteins are strongly enriched in MITFlow tumors even after removing samples with highest fibroblast marker expression.
source: However, to rule out the possibility that the increased expression of ECM genes in TCGA MITFlow melanoma tumors was derived from fibroblast cells, we removed the 130 melanoma TCGA samples that showed the highest expression of the fibroblast markers PDGFRB and ACTA2 and then assessed the expression of collagens across the 30 MITF highest and lowest melanoma samples, which consistently showed that expression of genes encoding ECM proteins are strongly enriched in MITFlow tumors (Figure 3i).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of fibroblast-depleted TCGA data shown in Figure 3i

claim: The enrichment for ECM genes was observed in both primary and metastatic tumors.
source: The enrichment for ECM genes was observed in both primary and metastatic tumors (Figure 3i).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3i

claim: There was no correlation between MITF expression and the most common BRAF, NRAS, and NF1 mutations found in melanoma.
source: We did not observe a correlation between MITF expression and the most common BRAF, NRAS, and NF1 mutations found in melanoma (Figure 3j), indicating that the gene expression changes observed are controlled via transcriptional regulation, directly or indirectly imposed by MITF.
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA mutation data shown in Figure 3j

claim: The expression of CDH2 (N-cadherin) was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors (R = −0.3, p<1.9e-11).
source: As expected the analysis of the TCGA data showed that the expression of CDH2 (N-cadherin) (R = −0.3, p<1.9e-11), TGFB1(R = −0.49, p<2.2e-16) and ZEB1 (R = −0.41, p<2.2e-16) was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors, whereas the expression of CDH1 (R = 0.42, p<2.2e-16) and SLUG (SNAI2) (R = 0.43, p<2.2e-16) was positively correlated (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4a

claim: The expression of TGFB1 was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors (R = −0.49, p<2.2e-16).
source: As expected the analysis of the TCGA data showed that the expression of CDH2 (N-cadherin) (R = −0.3, p<1.9e-11), TGFB1(R = −0.49, p<2.2e-16) and ZEB1 (R = −0.41, p<2.2e-16) was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors, whereas the expression of CDH1 (R = 0.42, p<2.2e-16) and SLUG (SNAI2) (R = 0.43, p<2.2e-16) was positively correlated (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4a

claim: The expression of ZEB1 was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors (R = −0.41, p<2.2e-16).
source: As expected the analysis of the TCGA data showed that the expression of CDH2 (N-cadherin) (R = −0.3, p<1.9e-11), TGFB1(R = −0.49, p<2.2e-16) and ZEB1 (R = −0.41, p<2.2e-16) was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors, whereas the expression of CDH1 (R = 0.42, p<2.2e-16) and SLUG (SNAI2) (R = 0.43, p<2.2e-16) was positively correlated (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4a

claim: The expression of CDH1 was positively correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors (R = 0.42, p<2.2e-16).
source: As expected the analysis of the TCGA data showed that the expression of CDH2 (N-cadherin) (R = −0.3, p<1.9e-11), TGFB1(R = −0.49, p<2.2e-16) and ZEB1 (R = −0.41, p<2.2e-16) was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors, whereas the expression of CDH1 (R = 0.42, p<2.2e-16) and SLUG (SNAI2) (R = 0.43, p<2.2e-16) was positively correlated (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4a

claim: The expression of SLUG (SNAI2) was positively correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors (R = 0.43, p<2.2e-16).
source: As expected the analysis of the TCGA data showed that the expression of CDH2 (N-cadherin) (R = −0.3, p<1.9e-11), TGFB1(R = −0.49, p<2.2e-16) and ZEB1 (R = −0.41, p<2.2e-16) was anti-correlated with MITF in melanoma tumors, whereas the expression of CDH1 (R = 0.42, p<2.2e-16) and SLUG (SNAI2) (R = 0.43, p<2.2e-16) was positively correlated (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4a

claim: The expression of the CDH1 and SNAI2 genes was reduced in MITFlow tumors and ΔMITF-X6 cells.
source: Consistent with this, the expression of the CDH1 and SNAI2 genes was reduced in MITFlow tumors and ΔMITF-X6 cells, whereas the expression of CDH2, SOX2, TGFß1, and ZEB1 was increased (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b

claim: The expression of CDH2, SOX2, TGFß1, and ZEB1 was increased in MITFlow tumors and ΔMITF-X6 cells.
source: Consistent with this, the expression of the CDH1 and SNAI2 genes was reduced in MITFlow tumors and ΔMITF-X6 cells, whereas the expression of CDH2, SOX2, TGFß1, and ZEB1 was increased (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b

claim: Increased expression of CDH2 was observed upon siRNA-mediated KD of MITF in SkMel28 and 501Mel cells.
source: We also observed increased expression of CDH2 upon siRNA-mediated KD of MITF in SkMel28 and 501Mel cells; however, the level of CDH1 was decreased only in the siMITF SkMel28 cells (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b

claim: Upon MITF overexpression in the pB-MITF-FLAG A375P cells, the expression of CDH2, SNAI2, SOX2, and TGFß1 was decreased, whereas the expression of CDH1 and ZEB1 was increased.
source: Interestingly, upon MITF overexpression in the pB-MITF-FLAG A375P cells, the expression of CDH2, SNAI2, SOX2, and TGFß1 was decreased, whereas the expression of CDH1 and ZEB1 was increased (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b

claim: CDH1 expression was reduced 50- and 100-fold in the ∆MITF-X2 and ∆MITF-X6 cells, respectively, when compared to EV-SkMel28 cells.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of EMT genes in the MITF-KO cells confirmed that CDH1 expression was reduced 50- and 100-fold in the ∆MITF-X2 and ∆MITF-X6 cells, respectively, whereas CDH2 and TGFß1 were significantly increased when compared to EV-SkMel28 cells (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4c

claim: CDH2 and TGFß1 were significantly increased in MITF-KO cells when compared to EV-SkMel28 cells.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of EMT genes in the MITF-KO cells confirmed that CDH1 expression was reduced 50- and 100-fold in the ∆MITF-X2 and ∆MITF-X6 cells, respectively, whereas CDH2 and TGFß1 were significantly increased when compared to EV-SkMel28 cells (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4c

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed increased expression of the classical EMT marker protein CDH2 and decreased expression of CDH1 in both MITF-KO cell lines.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed increased expression of the classical EMT marker protein CDH2 and decreased expression of CDH1 in both MITF-KO cell lines (Figure 4d,e).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4d,e

claim: ZEB1, SOX2, CDH1, and CDH2 genes contain MITF-binding peaks in their intronic and promoter regions.
source: Analysis of CUT and RUN and publicly available MITF ChIP-seq data showed that ZEB1, SOX2, CDH1, and CDH2 genes contain MITF-binding peaks in their intronic and promoter regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d; Laurette et al., 2015), whereas TGFß1 does not.
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d and cited from Laurette et al., 2015

claim: TGFß1 does not contain MITF-binding peaks.
source: Analysis of CUT and RUN and publicly available MITF ChIP-seq data showed that ZEB1, SOX2, CDH1, and CDH2 genes contain MITF-binding peaks in their intronic and promoter regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d; Laurette et al., 2015), whereas TGFß1 does not.
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN and ChIP-seq data

claim: The expression of all four genes (CDH2, ID1, MMP15, CDH1) was partially rescued upon introducing the MITF-FLAG construct into ΔMITF-X6 cells.
source: Importantly, the expression of all four genes was partially rescued upon introducing the MITF-FLAG construct into ΔMITF-X6 cells; a smaller rescue effect was observed in ΔMITF-X2 cells transfected with MITF-FLAG (Figure 5a–d).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 5a-d

claim: MITF mRNA and protein expression was significantly decreased after 24 hr of dox treatment and reached basal levels again 96 hr after dox removal.
source: Our results showed that MITF mRNA and protein expression was significantly decreased after 24 hr of dox treatment and reached basal levels again 96 hr after dox removal (Figure 5f,g), showing that the dox-inducible system is suitable for reversibly modulating MITF levels.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5f,g

claim: CDH1 mRNA expression decreased sharply after 24 hr of dox treatment and gradually increased 72 and 96 hr after dox removal, consistent with the restoration of MITF expression.
source: We observed a sharp decrease in CDH1 mRNA expression after 24 hr of dox treatment. However, 72 and 96 hr after dox removal its expression had gradually increased, consistent with the restoration of MITF expression (Figure 5g).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5g

claim: The expression of CDH2, SERPINA3, and ITGA2 was sharply increased after 24 hr of dox treatment and decreased again 96 hr after dox removal.
source: Similarly, the expression of genes repressed by MITF such as CDH2, SERPINA3, and ITGA2 was sharply increased after 24 hr of dox treatment and decreased again 96 hr after dox removal (Figure 5h–j).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5h-j

claim: After 72 and 96 hr of dox removal, MITF expression was restored and expression of the E-Cadherin protein was increased back to initial levels, whereas the expression of N-Cadherin was reduced compared to that observed at 24 hr of MITF KD.
source: After 72 and 96 hr of dox removal, MITF expression was restored and expression of the E-Cadherin protein was increased back to initial levels, whereas the expression of N-Cadherin was reduced compared to that observed at 24 hr of MITF KD (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5f

claim: Immunostaining revealed an increased number of paxillin (PXN)-positive focal points around the cell periphery of MITF-KO cells as compared to EV-SkMel28 control cells.
source: Indeed, immunostaining revealed an increased number of paxillin (PXN)-positive focal points (stained using PXN phospho -Tyr118 antibodies) around the cell periphery of MITF-KO cells as compared to EV-SkMel28 control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a

claim: Quantification of the focal points showed around twofold increase in their numbers in both MITF-KO cell lines.
source: Quantification of the focal points showed around twofold increase in their numbers in both MITF-KO cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b

claim: Transcriptomic data of the 473 melanoma tumor samples from TCGA showed a significant negative correlation between the expression of MITF and PXN in these samples.
source: Transcriptomic data of the 473 melanoma tumor samples from TCGA showed a significant negative correlation between the expression of MITF and PXN in these samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c

claim: Expression of PXN was specifically induced in MITFlow melanoma cell lines and displayed a negative correlation with MITF expression in a panel of 163 patient-derived melanoma cells.
source: We also assessed the expression of PXN in a panel of 163 patient-derived melanoma cells exhibiting different levels of MITF. This showed that expression of PXN was specifically induced in MITFlow melanoma cell lines and displayed a negative correlation with MITF expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: Supported by analysis of patient-derived melanoma cell line data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e

claim: After a 24 hr induction of MITF KD, a twofold increase was observed in the number of PXN-positive focal points at the cell borders when compared to the miR-NTC control cell lines.
source: After a 24 hr induction of MITF KD, a twofold increase was observed in the number of PXN-positive focal points at the cell borders when compared to the miR-NTC control cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f–h).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f-h

claim: ChIP-seq data showed an MITF peak in intron 6 of PXN containing the CACGTG motif.
source: Analysis of ChIP-seq data showed an MITF peak in intron 6 of PXN containing the CACGTG motif (Figure 6—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1i

claim: Treating EV-SkMel28 cells with vemurafenib led to a decrease in MITF protein expression.
source: Indeed, treating the cells with vemurafenib led to a decrease in MITF protein expression in EV-SkMel28 cells which is consistent with the literature.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and consistent with literature

claim: The expression of MITF in the 501Mel cell upon vemurafenib treatment was increased compared to a DMSO control.
source: However, the expression of MITF in the 501Mel cell upon vemurafenib treatment was increased compared to a DMSO control (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a,b

claim: The MITF-KO cells showed a fourfold increase in the number of focal adhesions as compared to EV-SkMel28 cells under the control DMSO-treated conditions.
source: Consistent with the observation above, the MITF-KO cells showed a fourfold increase in the number of focal adhesions as compared to EV-SkMel28 cells under the control DMSO-treated conditions (Figure 6a (upper panel), b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6a,b

claim: Treatment with vemurafenib resulted in a significant increase in the number of focal adhesions in the EV-SkMel28 cells but a further increase was also observed in the MITF-KO cells.
source: Treatment with vemurafenib resulted in a significant increase in the number of focal adhesions in the EV-SkMel28 cells but a further increase was also observed in the MITF-KO cells (Figure 6a [lower panel], b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6a,b

claim: Knockdown of MITF induced through the miR-MITF construct in both 501Mel and SkMel28 cells led to an increased number of focal adhesions when compared to miR-NTC cells.
source: Consistent with this, knockdown of MITF induced through the miR-MITF construct in both 501Mel and SkMel28 cells led to an increased number of focal adhesions when compared to miR-NTC cells (Figure 6c,d [upper panels], e, f).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6c-f

claim: Treatment with vemurafenib further increased the number of focal adhesions in SkMel28 cells expressing miR-NTC or miR-MITF, but more focal points were observed in miR-MITF cells under these conditions.
source: Treatment with vemurafenib further increased the number of focal adhesions in SkMel28 cells expressing miR-NTC or miR-MITF, but again, more focal points were observed in miR-MITF cells under these conditions (Figure 6c,d [lower panels]).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6c,d

claim: Vemurafenib treatment alone did not lead to an increase in focal adhesion formation in 501Mel cells expressing miR-NTC, whereas a major increase in focal adhesions was observed upon MITF depletion in the miR-MITF cells.
source: Importantly, vemurafenib treatment alone did not lead to an increase in focal adhesion formation in 501Mel cells expressing miR-NTC which is consistent with increased MITF protein expression upon vemurafenib treatment, whereas a major increase in focal adhesions was observed upon MITF depletion in the miR-MITF cells (Figure 6c [lower panel], e).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6c,e

claim: After 72 hr of treatment with 10 µM of FAKi the viability of MITF-KO cells was significantly reduced compared to the EV-SkMel28 cells.
source: We observed that after 72 hr of treatment with 10 µM of FAKi the viability of MITF-KO cells was significantly reduced compared to the EV-SkMel28 cells; the effect of FAKi on ∆MITF-X6 cells was more pronounced than in ∆MITF-X2 cells (Figure 6g,h).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6g,h

claim: The effect of FAKi on ∆MITF-X6 cells was more pronounced than in ∆MITF-X2 cells.
source: We observed that after 72 hr of treatment with 10 µM of FAKi the viability of MITF-KO cells was significantly reduced compared to the EV-SkMel28 cells; the effect of FAKi on ∆MITF-X6 cells was more pronounced than in ∆MITF-X2 cells (Figure 6g,h).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6g,h

claim: ∆MITF-X6 cells were significantly enriched in the MRD gene signature.
source: Our GSEA analysis showed that ∆MITF-X6 cells were significantly enriched in the MRD gene signature but not with the invasive signature found in another sub-population of MRD cells in the xenografts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c

claim: ∆MITF-X6 cells were not enriched with the invasive signature found in another sub-population of MRD cells in the xenografts.
source: Our GSEA analysis showed that ∆MITF-X6 cells were significantly enriched in the MRD gene signature but not with the invasive signature found in another sub-population of MRD cells in the xenografts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c

claim: Among the genes that overlap between the MRD and ∆MITF-X6 cells are ECM genes such as COL4A1, ITGA1, ITGA6, LAMC1, and VCAN.
source: Among the genes that overlap between the MRD and ∆MITF-X6 cells are ECM genes such as COL4A1, ITGA1, ITGA6, LAMC1, and VCAN.
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene lists from GSEA analysis

claim: Single cell RNA-seq data of MITF-depleted zebrafish melanomas and bulk-RNA-seq data of MITFlow melanoma tumors showed positive enrichment with ∆MITF-X6 cells.
source: The same findings were obtained using single cell RNA-seq data of MITF-depleted zebrafish melanomas as well as bulk-RNA-seq data of MITFlow melanoma tumors (Travnickova et al., 2019). Both datasets showed positive enrichment with ∆MITF-X6 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of zebrafish data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2d and cited from Travnickova et al., 2019

claim: In the zebrafish data the ECM signature was specifically induced in the single cell cluster from MITF-low superficial tumors (representing minimal residual disease) compared to other single-cell clusters from MITF-high melanomas.
source: Importantly, we found that in the zebrafish data the ECM signature was specifically induced in the single cell cluster from MITF-low superficial tumors (representing minimal residual disease) compared to other single-cell clusters from MITF-high melanomas (Figure 6—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis of zebrafish single cell data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2e

claim: Both of the MITF-KO cells had a twofold reduction in proliferation rate as compared to the EV-SkMel28 cells.
source: This showed that both of the MITF-KO cells had a twofold reduction in proliferation rate as compared to the EV-SkMel28 cells (Figure 7a).
evidence: Supported by IncuCyte live cell imaging data shown in Figure 7a

claim: ∆MITF-X6 and ∆MITF-X2 cells had fewer (20–25%) BrdU-positive cells than the EV-SkMel28 cells (45%).
source: Second, a BrdU incorporation assay showed that ∆MITF-X6 and ∆MITF-X2 cells had fewer (20–25%) BrdU-positive cells than the EV-SkMel28 cells (45%), suggesting that there are fewer actively proliferating cells in the MITF-KO cells compared to the control cells (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by BrdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 7b

claim: The MITF-KO cells failed to close the wound in 24 hrs, whereas the EV-SkMel28 cells were able to close the wound within that time.
source: Strikingly, the wound scratch assay showed that the MITF-KO cells failed to close the wound in 24 hrs, whereas the EV-SkMel28 cells were able to close the wound within that time (Figure 7c,d).
evidence: Supported by wound scratch assay data shown in Figure 7c,d

claim: Upon MITF-KD, a minor decrease in the ability of the cells to close the wound was observed when compared to the control miR-NTC cells.
source: Upon MITF-KD, we observed a minor decrease in the ability of the cells to close the wound when compared to the control miR-NTC cells (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: Supported by wound scratch assay data shown in Figure 7e,f

claim: MITF-KO cells displayed a severe reduction in invasion ability compared to the EV-SkMel28 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that MITF-KO cells displayed a severe reduction in invasion ability compared to the EV-SkMel28 cells (Figure 7g,h).
evidence: Supported by transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 7g,h

claim: MITF acts as a transcriptional repressor of genes involved in ECM and focal adhesion.
source: In this study, we have shown that MITF directly binds to and represses the expression of ECM, EMT and focal adhesion genes in human melanoma cells.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including CUT-and-RUN, ChIP-seq, and gene expression studies

claim: A role for MITF as a repressor has been described in both melanoma cells and immune cells.
source: A role for MITF as a repressor has been described in both melanoma cells and immune cells (Riesenberg et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Riesenberg et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2007

claim: In myeloid precursor cells, MITF was shown to interact with EOS to recruit co-repressors to target genes.
source: In myeloid precursor cells, MITF was shown to interact with EOS to recruit co-repressors to target genes (Hu et al., 2007), whereas in melanoma cells MITF bound directly to an E-box located in an enhancer of the c-JUN gene, leading to reduced expression of the gene (Riesenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2007

claim: In melanoma cells MITF bound directly to an E-box located in an enhancer of the c-JUN gene, leading to reduced expression of the gene.
source: In myeloid precursor cells, MITF was shown to interact with EOS to recruit co-repressors to target genes (Hu et al., 2007), whereas in melanoma cells MITF bound directly to an E-box located in an enhancer of the c-JUN gene, leading to reduced expression of the gene (Riesenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Riesenberg et al., 2015

claim: Many of the genes whose expression is repressed by MITF are bound by MITF and contain E-boxes in their regulatory regions.
source: Our results show that many of the genes whose expression is repressed by MITF are bound by MITF and contain E-boxes in their regulatory regions (Figure 2h).
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN data and motif analysis shown in Figure 2h

claim: Knocking down MITF leads to a major increase in TGFß1 mRNA expression in the melanoma cells.
source: Our observations suggest that knocking down MITF leads to a major increase in TGFß1 mRNA expression in the melanoma cells, suggesting that the effects are cell-autonomous and driven by MITF.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq data

claim: There are no MITF-peaks in or near the TGFß1 gene in melanoma cells.
source: However, there are no MITF-peaks in or near the TGFß1 gene in melanoma cells, leading us to hypothesize that the effects must be mediated through a hitherto unknown intermediary.
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN and ChIP-seq data showing absence of MITF binding

claim: Enhanced expression and phosphorylation of paxillin has been linked to therapy resistance in lung cancer.
source: Enhanced expression and phosphorylation of paxillin has been linked to therapy resistance in other cancer cell types, such as lung cancer (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2016

claim: An inverse relation between BRAF inhibition and the expression of ECM genes has been described as a marker of de-differentiated drug-resistant cells in melanoma.
source: In melanoma, an inverse relation between BRAF inhibition and the expression of ECM genes has been described as a marker of de-differentiated drug-resistant cells (Fallahi-Sichani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fallahi-Sichani et al., 2017

claim: The number of paxillin-positive dots was induced in both MITF-KO and miR-MITF cells as compared to controls.
source: Our data showed that the number of paxillin-positive dots was induced in both MITF-KO and miR-MITF cells as compared to controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b,f,g h) and paxillin expression was inversely correlated with MITF expression in melanoma tissues and cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b,f,g,h

claim: Paxillin expression was inversely correlated with MITF expression in melanoma tissues and cell lines.
source: Our data showed that the number of paxillin-positive dots was induced in both MITF-KO and miR-MITF cells as compared to controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b,f,g h) and paxillin expression was inversely correlated with MITF expression in melanoma tissues and cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c-e

claim: An increase in the expression of several integrins including ITGA1, ITGA2, ITGA6, ITGA10, and ITGB3 was observed in the MITF-KO cells, as well as in the siMITF 501Mel and SkMel28 cell lines.
source: We observed an increase in the expression of several integrins including ITGA1, ITGA2, ITGA6, ITGA10, and ITGB3 in the MITF-KO cells, as well as in the siMITF 501Mel and SkMel28 cell lines (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data

claim: The FLT1 receptor tyrosine kinase (VEGFR1) and its ligand VEGFA, which activate a pathway that phosphorylates FAK, were increased in expression upon MITF loss.
source: In addition to this, the FLT1 receptor tyrosine kinase (VEGFR1) and its ligand VEGFA, which activate a pathway that phosphorylates FAK, a key mediator of focal adhesions, were increased in expression.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data

claim: Both FLT1 and VEGFA have MITF-binding sites in their promoters.
source: Interestingly, both FLT1 and VEGFA have MITF-binding sites in their promoters and MITF has previously been shown to regulate VEGFA expression (Louphrasitthiphol et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN/ChIP-seq data and citation to Louphrasitthiphol et al., 2019

claim: MITF has previously been shown to regulate VEGFA expression.
source: Interestingly, both FLT1 and VEGFA have MITF-binding sites in their promoters and MITF has previously been shown to regulate VEGFA expression (Louphrasitthiphol et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Louphrasitthiphol et al., 2019

claim: Exposure of melanoma cells to BRAF and MEK inhibitors has been shown to slow growth and result in increased expression of NGFR and ECM and focal adhesion genes.
source: Exposure of melanoma cells to BRAF and MEK inhibitors has been shown to slow growth and result in increased expression of NGFR and ECM and focal adhesion genes (Fallahi-Sichani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fallahi-Sichani et al., 2017

claim: An up to 200-fold induction of the NGFR transcript was observed in the MITF-KO cells compared to EV-SkMel28 cells.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed an up to 200-fold induction of the NGFR transcript in the MITF-KO cells compared to EV-SkMel28 cells, and we identified an MITF peak in the 3'UTR of NGFR in both the MITF CUT-and-RUN data from SkMel28 cells and in the MITF ChIP-seq data from COLO829 cells (Webster et al., 2014); expression of the melanocyte differentiation marker and MITF target MLANA was 50- to 80-fold reduced in the MITF-KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-d

claim: An MITF peak was identified in the 3'UTR of NGFR in both the MITF CUT-and-RUN data from SkMel28 cells and in the MITF ChIP-seq data from COLO829 cells.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed an up to 200-fold induction of the NGFR transcript in the MITF-KO cells compared to EV-SkMel28 cells, and we identified an MITF peak in the 3'UTR of NGFR in both the MITF CUT-and-RUN data from SkMel28 cells and in the MITF ChIP-seq data from COLO829 cells (Webster et al., 2014); expression of the melanocyte differentiation marker and MITF target MLANA was 50- to 80-fold reduced in the MITF-KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by CUT-and-RUN and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-d and cited from Webster et al., 2014

claim: Expression of the melanocyte differentiation marker and MITF target MLANA was 50- to 80-fold reduced in the MITF-KO cells.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed an up to 200-fold induction of the NGFR transcript in the MITF-KO cells compared to EV-SkMel28 cells, and we identified an MITF peak in the 3'UTR of NGFR in both the MITF CUT-and-RUN data from SkMel28 cells and in the MITF ChIP-seq data from COLO829 cells (Webster et al., 2014); expression of the melanocyte differentiation marker and MITF target MLANA was 50- to 80-fold reduced in the MITF-KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-d

claim: Cell survival of MITF-KO cells might be dependent on FAK pathway.
source: Importantly, we found that cell survival of MITF- KO cells might be dependent on FAK pathway (Figure 6g,h); therefore, this might be the therapeutic vulnerability of MITF-low melanoma cells and can potentially enhance the current treatment options of melanoma.
evidence: Supported by FAK inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 6g,h

claim: Changes in important EMT markers and regulators such as ZEB1, CDH1 (E-Cadherin), CDH2 (N-Cadherin), SNAI2, and TGFß1 were observed in the MITF-KO cells as well as in TCGA melanoma samples.
source: Indeed, we observed changes in important EMT markers and regulators such as ZEB1, CDH1 (E-Cadherin), CDH2 (N-Cadherin), SNAI2, and TGFß1 in the MITF-KO cells (Figure 4b–e) as well as in TCGA melanoma samples.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR, Western blot, and TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 4b-e

claim: The MITF-KO cells showed increased expression of SOX2, which is important for neuronal stem cell maintenance and has been suggested to be important for self-renewal of melanoma tumor cells.
source: Also, the MITF-KO cells showed increased expression of SOX2, which is important for neuronal stem cell maintenance and has been suggested to be important for self-renewal of melanoma tumor cells (Taranova et al., 2006; Santini et al., 2014; Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4b and citations to Taranova et al., 2006; Santini et al., 2014

claim: The effects of MITF on the expression of E-Cadherin, N-Cadherin, and ECM genes (ITGA2 and SERPINA3) is reversible.
source: Importantly, the effects of MITF on the expression of E-Cadherin, N-Cadherin, and ECM genes (ITGA2 and SERPINA3) is reversible (Figure 5e–j).
evidence: Supported by doxycycline-inducible MITF knockdown/restoration experiments shown in Figure 5e-j

claim: ∆MITF-X6 cells are positively correlated with the gene signature of a population of MRD cells in melanoma tumors as determined by single-cell RNA-seq of human PDX samples and zebrafish melanoma models.
source: We found that ∆MITF-X6 cells are positively correlated with the gene signature of a population of MRD cells in melanoma tumors as determined by single-cell RNA-seq of human PDX samples and zebrafish melanoma models (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c–e; Figure 2c; Rambow et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c-e and Figure 2c, and cited from Rambow et al., 2018

claim: The MRD melanoma cells in zebrafish express little to no MITF protein and have increased expression of ECM genes.
source: Interestingly, the MRD melanoma cells in zebrafish express little to no MITF protein and have increased expression of ECM genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Supported by analysis of zebrafish single cell data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2e

claim: The induced expression of ECM genes and low expression of MITF is one of the markers of MRD in melanoma.
source: This suggests that the induced expression of ECM genes and low expression of MITF is one of the markers of MRD in melanoma.
evidence: Based on inference from correlation with MRD gene signatures

claim: In the absence of MITF, melanoma cells may become MRD cells by reshaping their ECM, enhancing their attachment to the surface, thus forming quiescent cells which wait for an opportunity to change their phenotype and re-emerge as proliferative melanoma cells.
source: In the absence of MITF, melanoma cells may become MRD cells by reshaping their ECM, enhancing their attachment to the surface, thus forming quiescent cells which wait for an opportunity to change their phenotype and re-emerge as proliferative melanoma cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations and MRD correlation

claim: This process is cell-autonomous and under the direction of MITF which instructs the cells to create their own microenvironment.
source: Since melanoma cells can mediate these effects on their own, in the absence of the tumor microenvironment, this suggests that this process is cell-autonomous and under the direction of MITF which instructs the cells to create their own microenvironment.
evidence: Based on inference from observations in isolated cell culture
